newsitem.title: INDIA: Relatives of Western hostages arrive in Kashmir.
newsitem.headline: Relatives of Western hostages arrive in Kashmir.

text.p: Relatives of three of four Western hostages arrived in Kashmir on Sunday, a day after the Himalayan territory's Indian chief minister Farooq Abdullah said he had reports they were still alive.

Jane Schelly, wife of American hostage Donald Hutchings, Julie Mangan, wife of Briton Keith Mangan, Catherine Mosley and Bob Wells, girlfriend and father of Briton Paul Wells, arrived in the state capital of Srinagar with diplomats.
"We have come to your beautiful valley to seek your help to know the whereabouts of our dear ones," a statement issued by relatives of the hostages said.
"We are dying to see them, they are away from us for the last 15 months and we want to know whether they are dead or alive," the statement said.

"We live in continuous pain without them and we hope that coming winter they will not spend away from us. If they are dead please return their bodies so that we can observe their last rites according to our rituals."

Wells and Mangan, Hutchings and German Dirk Hasert were abducted on July, 1995 by the little known Al-Faran group while trekking in southern Kashmir. The decapitated body of a fifth hostage, Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe, was found in a remote Kashmiri forest in August, 1995.
Authorities using sniffer dogs in June scoured a forest where a captured militant said he believed the hostages had been buried after being killed last year. The search found no clues.
Indian authorities have had no contact with Al-Faran since last November, and diplomats said they had no firm information to indicate whether the hostages are dead or alive.
Jammu and Kashmir state Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah said on Saturday he had reports that the four were still alive.
"According to the latest reports that we have received, all the four hostages are alive. I am trying to investigate into it," Abdullah told a news conference in Srinagar.
Kashmir's shadowy Al Faran militants kidnapped the men and demanded the release of jailed militant colleagues.

Abdullah, whose National Conference party won an absolute majority in last month's assembly elections, said he had some idea of the location where the hostages were believed to be held, but declined to give details.
Dozens of Kashmiri militant groups are fighting Indian rule in the disputed Himalayan state since 1990.
Abdullah said he was giving them 30 days to surrender but did not say if he would call a ceasfire during the period.
Police and hospital sources say at least 20,000 people have been killed in Kashmir's separatist violence. Abdullah said the total was closer to 50,000.
Abdullah's remarks on the hostages coincide with growing pessimism over their fate.
Western diplomats in Delhi said this month that the United States was considering offering a financial reward for information about the whereabouts of the hostages.
But Washington wanted first to clear the offer with Indian authorities and the other countries whose nationals are held.
British High Commissioner (ambassador) David Gore-Booth told reporters earlier this month there were reports that the hostages had recently been sighted.
But he said there was no firm information as to their whereabouts. "We have no proof of life or proof of death," he said.
Asked if diplomats were extremely gloomy, Gore-Booth said: "Yes."
